title: Negative questions; echo questions; questions with that-clauses

sections.title: Negative questions
sections.content:
We usually make a negative yes/no or wh-question with an auxiliary verb (have, did, would, etc.) + -n’t to suggest, persuade, criticise, etc.:
• Wouldn’t it be better to go tomorrow?
• Why don’t we go out for a meal?
In formal contexts, or when we want to give some special emphasis to the negative (perhaps to show that we are angry, very surprised, or to strongly persuade someone), we can use not after the subject in negative questions. This happens particularly in yes/no rather than wh-questions:
• Did she not realise that she'd broken it? (more emphatic than Didn't she realise that...?)
• Can you not get there a bit earlier? (more emphatic than Can't you...?)

sections.title: Negative words in questions
sections.content:
We sometimes use negative words instead of -n’t such as never, no, nobody, nothing, nowhere:
• Why do you never help?
• Have you nowhere to go? (or Do you have nowhere to go?)
Alternatively, but less emphatically or more informally:
• Why don’t you ever help?
• Haven’t you got anywhere to go? (or Don't you have anywhere...?)

sections.title: Suggestions with Why not and Why don’t
sections.content:
We can make a suggestion with Why not + bare infinitive or Why don’t / doesn’t + subject + bare infinitive (but not Why do not / does not...):
• Why not decorate the house yourself? (or Why don’t you decorate...?)
Why didn’t ... isn't used to make a suggestion, but can show that we think an action was wrong. For example, depending on intonation and context, it can be used to criticise someone:
• Why didn’t you tell me that in the first place? (I'm annoyed that you didn't)

sections.title: Negative questions for exclamations
sections.content:
We use negative question forms with falling intonation for exclamations when we expect agreement:
• Haven’t you grown!
• Doesn’t she look lovely!
• Didn’t it snow a lot!

sections.title: Echo questions
sections.content:
Echo questions are used when we haven't understood what has been said or to check that we heard correctly, perhaps because we found it very surprising. We might repeat, usually with a rising intonation, the whole of what was said:
• 'Tala's lost her job.' 'Tala's lost her job?'
or focus on part of what was said using a stressed wh-word or a phrase with how:
• 'Leon's arriving at 6:30.' 'When's Leon arriving? / Leon's arriving when?'
• 'We paid £3,000 for the painting.' 'How much did you pay? / You paid how much?'
We can use what or do + what to focus on the verb or part of the sentence beginning with the verb:
• 'I think she's having a sleep.' 'She's what?' (or 'She's doing what?')

sections.title: Questions with that-clauses
sections.content:
A wh-question can refer to a following that-clause, particularly after verbs such as expect, hope, reckon, say, suggest, suppose, and think. We can leave out that in these questions:
• When do you reckon (that) you'll finish the job?
However, when the wh-word is the subject, object or complement of the verb in the subordinate clause, we do not use that:
• What did you think was in the box? (not What did you think that was in the box?)

exercises.question: A: Can you lend me €10? B: Again? ___ got any money left? (... money left?)
exercises.hint: All are possible negative question forms.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: All of these
All are possible negative question forms. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: A: I'm annoyed that you didn't come to the meeting. B: Why? ___ my email on holiday? (... my email / on holiday?)
exercises.hint: Why didn't you check? (informal) or Why did you not check? (formal/emphatic).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both are possible
Why didn't you check? (informal) or Why did you not check? (formal/emphatic).

exercises.sentence: Didn't you never tell him the truth about what happened?
exercises.correction: Didn't you ever tell him the truth about what happened?
exercises.hint: Don't combine 'didn't' (negative auxiliary) with 'never' (negative adverb) — double negative.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Didn't you ever tell him the truth?
English standard grammar avoids double negatives. 'Didn't' is already negative, so use 'ever' (not 'never') to complete the negative question. Alternatively: 'Have you never told him?' — here 'have' is not negated so 'never' is correct.

exercises.question: A: I'll just finish my homework before I go to school. B: But ___ to finish it last night? (... be supposed to / last night?)
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both are possible
Negative question used for criticism/reminder.

exercises.question: A: ___ considered you might be wrong? / Have you ___ considered you might be wrong?
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Haven't you ever / never
Negative questions can use '-n't' + 'ever' or a positive question with 'never'. Both 'Haven't you ever considered it?' and 'Have you never considered it?' are correct and mean the same thing. 'Never' is the more emphatic form.

exercises.sentence: Hasn't she never been abroad before?
exercises.correction: Hasn't she ever been abroad before?
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Hasn't she ever been abroad before?
'Hasn't she never been' uses two negatives. Choose one: negative auxiliary ('hasn't') with 'ever', OR positive auxiliary ('has') with 'never'. Both convey the same meaning. 'Has she never been abroad?' is more emphatic; 'Hasn't she ever been?' is more conversational.

exercises.question: A: I spent the night in the railway station. B: ___ anywhere else to sleep? / Could you find ___ else to sleep?
A: Jake's going to Chile. B: He's going ___? / He's doing ___? / He's ___?
exercises.explanation:
Answer: where / what / what
In echo questions, you repeat the auxiliary verb from the statement and add the wh-word you want clarified. They show surprise or ask for confirmation. The wh-word (where/what/who) matches what information was unclear.

exercises.prompt: Form an echo question to express surprise:
exercises.hint: Echo question: auxiliary + subject + (adverb) + bare infinitive + object
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Did she really win the competition?
Echo questions repeat the structure of a statement as a question, often to express surprise or ask for confirmation. Use the auxiliary 'did' for past simple echo questions. 'Really' adds surprise/disbelief and typically comes after the subject.

exercises.question: A: He'll be away for three months. B: He'll be away for ___? / He'll ___?
exercises.explanation:
Answer: when / where
Choose the wh-word that matches the type of information you're asking about: 'when' for time, 'where' for place, 'how long' for duration, 'why' for reason. Echo the auxiliary from the original statement.

exercises.question: Was not it a brilliant film! (Correct the exclamation)
exercises.hint: Contracted form is standard for exclamations.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Wasn't it a brilliant film!
Contracted form is standard for exclamations. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: How do you think that Twitter will have changed our lives in ten years' time? (Improve the sentence)
options: How do you think Twitter will have changed...
How do you think that Twitter would have changed...
When do you think that Twitter will have changed...
exercises.hint: Remove 'that' in wh-questions where wh-word is part of the subordinate clause.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: How do you think Twitter will have changed...
Remove 'that' in wh-questions where wh-word is part of the subordinate clause. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).

exercises.question: A: Mariam isn't answering her phone. B: Why do you not email her? (Suggestion)
exercises.hint: Why not / Why don't you are more natural for suggestions.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both are better/natural
Why not / Why don't you are more natural for suggestions.
